newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil's Cardoso mired in political crisis.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil's Cardoso mired in political crisis.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso persuaded a key member of his administration not to quit Wednesday, but remained mired in a political crisis that threatens his already struggling reform program, analysts said.

Government officials and markets breathed a sigh of relief when a presidential aide said Deputy Luis Eduardo Magalhaes would not resign as chief whip in the lower house of Congress, contrary to a barrage of reports that he was standing down.
"The president asked him to stay, and he will remain leader," said the aide after Cardoso and Magalhaes met in the presidential palace.
Shares on the Sao Paulo stock exchange, which had slumped three percent on the reports of Magalhaes' resignation, recovered to end the morning up about 1.5 percent.

Magalhaes is a leading member of the Liberal Front Party (PFL), the strongest supporter of Cardoso's economic and structural reforms, and his father, Senator Antonio Carlos Magalhaes, is one of the most powerful figures in Congress.
As chief whip in the Chamber of Deputies, Luiz Eduardo oversees the government's painstaking attempts to get its reforms through Congress.

The PFL is also essential to Cardoso's hopes of winning re-election in next year's presidential elections. Party leaders have said they will not field a candidate and will support the president in 1998, just as they did in 1994.

But relations between the government and the PFL, which have often been tense, soured following publication Sunday of an interview by controversial Communications Minister Sergio Motta. He outraged an array of political figures by criticizing several government-allied parties, including the PFL.
Cardoso, seeking to snuff out the crisis quickly, summoned Motta to a meeting Monday.

But the minister, a long-time friend of the president who has survived several crises caused by his caustic opinions, was not forced to make a public apology. He then further enfuriated political rivals by cracking jokes at a jolly lunch Tuesday with fellow members of Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party.
"Our main problem is that the authority of the president is being undermined," said PFL Deputy Jose Carlos Aleluia. "Motta is playing with fire."

Ricardo Lopes, a consultant with Santa Fe Ideias in Brasilia, said the explosion of political rivalries would force Cardoso into taking a tougher line with his increasingly rowdy allies. "The obvious casualty is going to be the reform program, which is increasingly hard to implement," Lopes said.
The government has recently made some headway on two crucial reforms of the civil service and social security systems, both of which have been stuck in Congress for more than two years.
But even before this week's crisis, many observers questioned whether the government would manage to get the reforms through Congress before the October 1998 elections cloud the political scene.
Mauro Schneider, an economist with ING Barings in Sao Paulo, said he did not think Cardoso would bow to the PFL's pressure and sack Motta, one of his oldest friends.
Instead the government might have to win back support by negotiating some key points of its reforms.
"This is a hard blow for the government,but not a fatal one. The PFL won't leave the alliance because it's a pragmatic party and has nothing to gain in opposition," Schneider said.
